Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

vignette:
Tariq is a 55-year-old married farmer of Jordanian descent who has worked the same stretch of land in the Central Valley of California for nearly two decades. He came to the clinic at his wife's insistence, after months of what he described only as "not being right." His PCL-5 score of 76 places him in the severe range, and the picture that emerged across the first few sessions was of a man whose inner life had been profoundly reorganised by a single act of violence.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Tariq was attacked by a man he knew only loosely - a dispute over a boundary fence that had simmered for years before it turned physical. The assault happened at dusk, at the far edge of his property where no one could easily see or hear. The man came up behind him, and what Tariq remembers most vividly from that moment - before memory fractures into disconnected shards - is the sharp, sour smell of the other man's sweat and the sensation of his own heart slamming against his ribs as he struggled to break free. The attack left him with bruised ribs and a laceration, but the physical injuries healed in weeks. What did not heal was the way those two sensory details - the smell of sweat, the pounding in his chest - had been burned into him as signals of mortal danger.

In the months that followed, Tariq found that his own body had become unreliable. When he worked through the heat of the day and felt his heart rate climb, or caught the smell of his own perspiration, something in him would snap back to that dusk at the fence line, not as a coherent recollection but as a wave of alarm without clear shape. He also became acutely watchful of other people; when a farmhand lingered too long near a piece of equipment, or when a stranger moved in a way that seemed to lack a clear purpose, Tariq felt certain that something was about to happen. These moments of triggered arousal did not simply pass - they fed directly into a pattern of behaviour that, over time, became entrenched. When his heart raced and the fear surged, he would throw himself back into physical labour with an urgency that had nothing to do with the work itself. He drove the tractor longer than necessary, repaired fences that did not need repairing, and stayed in the fields past dark - not because the farm demanded it, but because motion and exhaustion were the only things that quieted the alarm. His wife noticed that he was no longer coming to dinner, that he had stopped sitting with her in the evenings, and that the distance between them had grown into something she could not name.

The memory itself presents its own difficulty and adds its own fuel to these patterns. Tariq cannot tell the story of the assault in a way that holds together. He begins, loses the thread, and stops - not because he is unwilling but because the event does not exist for him as a continuous narrative. It comes in pieces: the smell, the weight of a hand on his shoulder, a sound he cannot identify, then nothing, then the ground. When he tries to make sense of it, the whole thing feels strangely foreign, as though it happened to a man he once knew rather than to himself. This alienation from the memory does not bring relief; instead, it leaves him with an unresolved anger that has nowhere to go. He finds himself rehearsing, in elaborate detail, what he would do if he encountered the man again - mapping out confrontations, calculating responses. The rumination does not resolve anything, but it feels, at least, like a form of agency in the face of something that still does not fully feel real to him. He avoids the anniversary of the attack with careful deliberateness, rerouting his schedule for that entire week.

What finally brought Tariq to the clinic was a morning when he felt his heart race during routine irrigation work and spent the next four hours unable to leave the tractor cab. He told the intake clinician, quietly, that he did not recognise himself anymore. What he is most afraid of, he said, is that this is simply who he is now.
